source: Paraphrased from the team's 18 manual R1 test sessions (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-11). The candidate is 'Alex'; no names, session ids or verbatim candidate sentences.

opening.kind: short intro: name + years + list of past edtech firms
opening.description: The first reply to Christy's opener is one or two sentences: name, total years in sales, two or three edtech employers, no story and no numbers. It is a complete but thin answer; the bot has to pick a follow-up rather than wait for more.
examples: Sure, I'm Alex, roughly eight years in sales, all of it at a few online-learning companies.
Hi, Alex here. Six years selling courses at a couple of edtech outfits.
Eight-plus years for me; most recently at one ed-learning firm and before that another one.
opening.frequency: 10 of the 12 sessions where the candidate spoke (M01, M03, M05-M10, S07, S08); M02 and M04 led with numbers instead (opening-4)
opening.typical_timing: Starts 27-50 s after the opener begins, i.e. 1-6 s after Christy's ~25-30 s opener ends
opening.bot_should: Thank briefly, reflect one concrete detail (years or sector) without inflated praise, and ask one open follow-up (what they sold, what a typical day looked like).

opening.kind: splits the intro across 2-4 turns with pauses and a sign-off
opening.description: Candidate states years, pauses 5-20 s, adds the companies, then numbers, then a closing tag like 'that's me'. In M09 and M10 Christy started replying on the first fragment and was cut off when the candidate resumed.
examples: I'm Alex, about seven years in. ... Before this I was at a couple of edtech places, always as an advisor.
Deal sizes were roughly $700 to $2,000 and I closed ten or twelve a month. ... So yeah, that's me.
Eleven years, all of it sales. ... The companies were all in online education.
opening.bot_should: Hold the floor through short pauses after an unfinished clause; take the turn on a sign-off ('that's me', 'that's about it') or a clearly complete sentence. Never start the reply on a fragment.

opening.kind: greets back / opens with a pleasantry
opening.description: Candidate returns the greeting or adds a filler before the background ('hi, good evening', 'yeah, of course', 'oh, nice one'), sometimes noting Christy already knows their name.
examples: Hi, good evening. I'm Alex, which you already have on screen.
Yeah, of course. Hi there.
Oh, nice one. So, about me...
opening.typical_timing: First words of the first reply
opening.bot_should: No separate reply to the greeting; fold it into the acknowledgement of the background.

opening.kind: quotes hard numbers in the very first answer
opening.description: Candidate leads with revenue share, ticket size or monthly closure targets. Gives Christy an easy, specific follow-up hook.
examples: Three years at one edtech firm, and I alone brought in about 7% of company revenue.
Tickets ran between seven hundred and two thousand dollars; my monthly goal was ten to twelve closures.
opening.bot_should: Pick one number and ask how they achieved it or what drove it.

opening.kind: testers vary the persona: experience from 11 months to 11 years, or a non-edtech domain
opening.description: Across runs the team changed the background on purpose: 11 months (M07), 3 years (M04), 5 (M02, M03), 6 (M01), 7 (M08), 8 (M05, M06, M09, S07, S08), 11 (M10); one claimed insurance sales to individuals (M06). Checks that Christy's follow-ups and praise scale to the person (M07's bot called 11 months 'solid experience').
examples: I've only been in sales about eleven months, across three edtech firms.
Eleven years, every one of them in sales.
I mostly sold insurance policies to individual customers.
opening.frequency: All 12 speaking sessions vary it; junior (under 1 year) 1, non-edtech domain 1
opening.bot_should: Calibrate: no 'solid/strong experience' for under a year; for a different domain ask what transfers to course sales.

opening.kind: silent after the opener (no audio at all)
opening.description: Candidate never speaks. Christy asks 'are you still with me?' at ~55 s and ends at ~1:17 citing a lost connection. Four such runs back to back on one morning look like deliberate no-audio / mic-permission tests.
examples: [no speech at all for 75 s]
[no speech; tab stays open]
opening.typical_timing: Whole opening; bot nudge at ~0:55, bot ends at ~1:17
opening.bot_should: Run a sound check / mic hint first ('I can't hear you yet, check your mic'), give a second nudge, then end politely; do not claim the candidate left if the mic simply never opened.

opening.kind: leaves during or right after the opener
opening.description: Only Christy's opener exists; the candidate closes the tab before answering.
examples: [disconnects within ~30 s, no speech]
opening.bot_should: Record candidate_left cleanly; nothing to say. Simulator: disconnect at a random point in the opener.

opening.kind: talks while muted or with flaky mic, then 'can you hear me?' over background chatter
opening.description: In S07 the candidate gave an intro, Christy then said the mic seemed muted, and the next turn was regional-language side talk (about a bike and a watch) with a muddled 'can you hear me?'; the session died there. In M06 the mute aside fired ~6 s after a question, before any reply, and the candidate answered 'I am ready' (icebreaker-11).
examples: [side chatter in another language] ... hello, you can hear me, right?
Am I audible now?
opening.bot_should: If the transcript already holds the candidate's words, do not claim the mic is muted; say what was caught and ask for the rest. Ignore non-English background speech.

icebreaker.kind: one-line or one-word answers
icebreaker.description: Candidate answers a follow-up with a fragment or a single word, often to 'give me an example' questions. Tests whether Christy probes once and moves on instead of repeating the same question.
examples: I just pitch to people and get things started.
The selling part.
Yeah.
Yes, sir.
icebreaker.typical_timing: 0:50-3:30, mostly after an example or 'what did you enjoy' question
icebreaker.bot_should: One gentle, differently worded probe for specifics; if still thin, move on. Do not repeat the identical question.

icebreaker.kind: refuses or skips a question (sometimes twice in a row)
icebreaker.description: Candidate declines to share an example. M03 refused two consecutive questions.
examples: I'd rather not get into that one.
Let me pass on that question.
Not keen to answer that, honestly.
icebreaker.typical_timing: 2:28-3:10, always on 'tell me about a time you turned around a hesitant customer'
icebreaker.bot_should: Accept without pressure or comment ('no problem'), switch to an easier question; after two refusals consider moving to the brief.

icebreaker.kind: asks to jump straight to the role-play
icebreaker.description: Candidate wants to skip the get-to-know-you part.
examples: Could we just skip ahead to the role-play part?
Can we go straight into the mock call?
icebreaker.bot_should: Acknowledge, say the role-play comes in a couple of minutes, ask one more question; do not stonewall or lecture.

icebreaker.kind: asks Christy to repeat the question
icebreaker.description: Candidate missed or forgot the question. In M06 Christy launched the role-play brief instead of repeating, and the candidate kept asking for the question in the transition.
examples: Sorry, could you say the question once more?
Can you ask me that again?
icebreaker.typical_timing: Any time; also as the last icebreaker turn
icebreaker.bot_should: Repeat it in shorter words even when the icebreaker budget is spent, or say plainly 'let's move on to the role-play' first.

icebreaker.kind: contradicts own experience or background
icebreaker.description: Years change between answers (5 then 8; 8 then 10) or the domain shifts (edtech firms, then insurance). M03's bot clarified once, neutrally; M09's ignored it.
examples: I've been a program manager in sales for eight years (after saying five earlier).
In all my ten years of selling... (after saying eight).
Those were edtech companies, but I was selling insurance to retail clients.
icebreaker.typical_timing: 1:00-2:30, usually in the 'why this role' answer
icebreaker.bot_should: Ask once, neutrally, which figure is right; never accuse; accept the correction.

icebreaker.kind: long success story with numbers, split by pauses
icebreaker.description: A 30-75 s story about a hesitant buyer: several follow-ups, a reframe on value or ROI, an EMI or scholarship, a sale landing at month-end, a laid-off lead who got placed.
examples: One prospect kept stalling on payment; after calls, emails and a video meeting I reframed it around what he'd lose by waiting, and he paid roughly $3,000 right at month-end.
A client wanted a pricey course, around three lakh rupees, so my manager approved a scholarship and he signed.
A laid-off lead had a weak resume; I went through it, booked a consult, pointed him to interview prep, and he got hired.
icebreaker.bot_should: Do not barge in at mid-story pauses; acknowledge one specific detail and ask what they learned or move to the next topic.

icebreaker.kind: keeps talking as Christy starts her next line ('one more thing...')
icebreaker.description: Candidate adds to the previous answer just as Christy begins. In M02 and M04 the role-play brief started on top of the candidate.
examples: Wait, wait, there's one more thing I want to add...
...and mainly for growth, a fresh team, picking up new skills.
icebreaker.bot_should: Yield, let them finish, then bridge into the brief. Never start the brief over the candidate.

icebreaker.kind: presence check when Christy is slow ('are you there?', 'hello?')
icebreaker.description: After ~8-12 s of no reply, or when Christy's line is cut, the candidate checks the line. Happens in every phase.
examples: Hello? You still there?
Hey, are you with me?
Hello... (mid-answer)
Christy, can you hear me?
icebreaker.frequency: 7 of 12 across all phases (M01, M05, M06, M07, M08, M10, S07); in the icebreaker itself 3 (M05, M06, M10)
icebreaker.typical_timing: After a bot delay of 8-12 s; M05 at 1:28
icebreaker.bot_should: Answer at once ('yes, I'm here') and continue with the pending line; cut the latency.

icebreaker.kind: fills silence with stray acknowledgements ('thank you', 'sorry', 'okay')
icebreaker.description: Short tokens as separate turns, either before an answer or after finishing one when Christy is slow.
examples: Thanks.
Sorry.
Okay.
Fine, yeah.
icebreaker.typical_timing: Right after Christy's question, or 3-10 s after the candidate's own answer
icebreaker.bot_should: Not an answer: after Christy's question keep waiting; after the candidate's own completed answer, respond now.

icebreaker.kind: setup question: camera on or off, can we pause
icebreaker.description: Questions about the interview setup itself.
examples: Should my camera be on, or is off fine?
Can we hold for a minute? Give me a second.
icebreaker.typical_timing: Anywhere; M06 at 3:11, M09 right after the intro (untimed)
icebreaker.bot_should: Answer in one line (camera optional; can't pause but can go at their pace) and re-ask the pending question.

icebreaker.kind: says 'I'm ready' outside the transition
icebreaker.description: After the mute aside the candidate said 'I am ready' meaning 'I'm back'. Must not start the role-play.
examples: Okay, I'm ready.
icebreaker.typical_timing: Reply to a mute or presence prompt
icebreaker.bot_should: Treat as 'I'm back', continue the icebreaker.

icebreaker.kind: motivation: 'sales is all I know' / growth / heard good things
icebreaker.description: Answer to 'why this role': sales is their only skill, they don't want a new domain, they want growth and a new team, or they heard incentives and culture are good.
examples: Sales is the only thing I've ever done, so I'm sticking with what I'm best at.
I don't want to switch domains at this stage, so an advisor role suits me.
Heard the incentives and the culture there are good, so thought I'd try.
Same job I do now, really; I just want a new team and room to grow.
icebreaker.bot_should: Accept, maybe one follow-up on what they enjoy; no challenge, no praise inflation.

icebreaker.kind: describes the daily grind with activity metrics
icebreaker.description: Lead lists, dial and connect targets, talk time, a playbook, booking a video call, CRM prep; often a 30-60 s process monologue.
examples: I get a lead list each morning, dial 120 to 150 numbers and aim for roughly two hours of talk time.
We had dial and connect percentages to hit, followed a playbook, booked a video call, then enrolled them.
Before an inbound call I open the lead's history in the CRM so I know what was said before.
icebreaker.typical_timing: 0:50-2:30, answer to 'what did a typical day look like'
icebreaker.bot_should: Pick one metric or step and ask how they handle a hesitant lead.

icebreaker.kind: claims empathy / rapport as the core strength
icebreaker.description: Candidate names empathy, rapport, listening, putting themselves in the learner's shoes.
examples: What I like most is building rapport and seeing things from the learner's side.
I'm very empathetic; I connect with people and try to fix their problems.
I enjoy listening to learners and finding where their gap is.
icebreaker.bot_should: Ask for a concrete example (expect icebreaker-1 or icebreaker-2 in response).

icebreaker.kind: target-attainment and performance claims
icebreaker.description: Percent of target, never on a performance plan, top performer for N months, closures per month.
examples: I was accountable for 70% of team revenue and we hit full target every month.
Never been on a PIP; top performer three months straight at my last place.
Ten to twelve closures a month was my number.
icebreaker.bot_should: Ask what they personally did to hit it (M01's bot did this well).

icebreaker.kind: abstract reflection instead of an example, after a long think
icebreaker.description: To 'a deal that didn't close', the candidate thinks ~20 s, then gives a philosophy (focus on the present, not the outcome).
examples: Lots of deals slipped and lots closed when I least expected; I just focus on the person in front of me, not the result.
icebreaker.bot_should: Do not fire 'are you still with me?' during a ~20 s think after a reflective question; accept the answer.

icebreaker.kind: inbound vs outbound and which is harder
icebreaker.description: Candidate handles both; finds inbound harder because they must read history while building rapport.
examples: Both: follow-ups I dial out, interested leads ring in.
Inbound's tougher, I'm reading their history while trying to build rapport.
icebreaker.bot_should: Natural follow-up on preparation; fine as the last icebreaker topic.

icebreaker.kind: B2B deal via referral, called 'easy'
icebreaker.description: A large account (500 staff) won through a contact; candidate downplays effort.
examples: Closed a 500-person public-sector account through someone in my network; it was an easy one.
icebreaker.bot_should: Ask what they did once introduced; don't over-praise.

icebreaker.kind: speech-recognition noise inside answers
icebreaker.description: Stray tokens ('bye', 'hello', 'see', 'right'), half-words and brand names mangled two ways in one session appear mid-answer. A stray 'bye' must never be read as a goodbye.
examples: [answer ends with a stray 'bye, sir' tacked on]
[a random product phrase dropped into a sentence about needs]
[stray 'hello' or 'see' in the middle of a sentence]
icebreaker.frequency: 7 of 12 across phases (M04, M05, M06, M07, M08, M10, S07)
icebreaker.bot_should: Ignore stray tokens; do not trigger end-intent or presence logic on them.

icebreaker.kind: numbers palette the testers used in the background part
icebreaker.description: Reference numbers for simulator variety.
examples: Experience: 11 months, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11 years
120-150 dials a day, ~120 minutes talk time; ticket $700-$2,000; 10-12 sales a month; one $3,000 sale
70% / 100% of target; 7% of company revenue; never on a PIP; top performer 3 months; a 500-person account; a course of about three lakh rupees
icebreaker.bot_should: Reflect numbers accurately if referenced; never invent numbers the candidate did not say.

icebreaker.kind: leaves during the icebreaker
icebreaker.description: S08 answered a 'tell me about a time' question with a bare 'yes, sir', Christy moved on, and the candidate was gone ~1:40 in. S07 left after the mic trouble (opening-8).
examples: Yes, sir. [then disconnects]
[side chatter, then disconnects]
icebreaker.bot_should: Record candidate_left; simulator should include an early quit after a thin answer.

transition.kind: asks for the brief again (often twice)
transition.description: Right after the ~40 s brief the candidate asks for it again because they lost focus. In M03 and M04 Christy answered 'whenever you're ready, just say ready' instead of repeating; in M04 the learner then picked up while the candidate was still asking.
examples: Could you run through the role-play setup again? I'd like more detail.
Just tell me the role-play part again.
Say again what you told me about the learner; I drifted off.
Christy, can you go over those instructions once more?
transition.frequency: 3 of 10 role-play sessions (M01 three times, M03, M04)
transition.bot_should: Re-deliver a recap (learner name and city, course, form a few days ago, you are the advisor calling back, goal, time limit, how to start), then ask 'ready, or any questions?' once.

transition.kind: asks for a shorter version of the brief
transition.description: Candidate wants a 3-4 line summary instead of the full brief.
examples: Can you give me that in about four lines?
Explain this round to me briefly, just a short summary.
transition.bot_should: A 3-4 sentence recap, not the full brief again.

transition.kind: asks about the company or the advisor job before starting
transition.description: Candidate asks to put questions first (asked three times in M02). Christy said 'say ready', then the learner picked up and treated the job question as an in-character line ('I'm calling about the course, not a job').
examples: Before the role-play, could I ask a couple of things?
First I'd like to know a bit more about the job itself.
Tell me about the company and this advisor position before we begin.
transition.bot_should: Answer from approved role information, then 'shall we start?'. Never start the role-play while a question is pending.

transition.description: Asked about 'the role play again'; Christy answered with job shift timings; candidate corrected that they meant the role-play scenario.
examples: No, I meant the role-play with the learner, not the job; tell me that part again.
transition.bot_should: In the transition, 'role play' or 'this round' means the scenario brief, not job terms.

examples: Ready.
I'm ready.
Yeah, ready.
Yes, I'm ready.
transition.typical_timing: 35-45 s after the brief starts (just after it ends) or after a repeated brief

transition.kind: starts without speaking (button) / role-play starts with no 'ready'
transition.description: M01 said nothing after the repeated brief and the learner picked up as it ended (button or auto-start); M09 has no candidate turn at all. In M02, M04 and M06 the learner picked up while the candidate was still asking for information.
examples: [silence, then presses I'm-ready]
[still asking a question when the learner says hello]
transition.frequency: 5 of 10 (M01, M09 silent start; M02, M04, M06 mis-start)
transition.bot_should: Start only on 'ready' or the button; if a question is pending, answer it first.

transition.kind: asks to go back to an icebreaker question
transition.description: Candidate wants the question they missed re-asked (twice), after Christy skipped their repeat request.
examples: Go back to the question before last and ask it again.
No, return to that earlier question and repeat it.
transition.bot_should: Either re-ask it briefly or explain plainly that we've moved on; never ignore it.

transition.kind: talks over the brief (still answering the last question)
transition.description: Candidate continues their 'why this role' answer while the brief plays, then asks for the brief.
examples: ...anyway, it's for my growth. Okay, can you explain this round again?
transition.bot_should: Stop the brief or re-deliver it after the candidate finishes.

transition.kind: noise words in the transition ('so bye', 'no option')
transition.description: Speech-recognition fragments that look like end or refusal intent.
examples: So bye.
No option.
transition.bot_should: Not end-intent and not 'ready'; wait or ask 'ready, or any questions?'.

roleplay.kind: casual greeting to the learner ('what's up?')
roleplay.description: Very informal opener.
examples: Hey [learner], what's happening?
Yo [learner], how's things?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner answers naturally and mentions the form.

roleplay.kind: polite warm greeting / how are you (sometimes repeated)
roleplay.description: Standard opener; M10 repeated the greeting after a stray remark.
examples: Hi [learner], how are you? Hope all's well.
Hello [learner], how's your day going?
Hey [learner], doing okay?
roleplay.bot_should: Short reply (e.g. a bit tired after work), let the advisor lead.

roleplay.kind: claims to have seen the learner's site activity / lead landed in my queue
roleplay.description: Advisor invents tracking ('you spent a lot of time on our data science page', 'your profile came into my bucket') and asks what brought her.
examples: I noticed you'd been spending quite a while on our data science page.
Your profile dropped into my list, and I can see you've been browsing our site.
I see you signed up for our webinar and looked at a few programs.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner confirms only what is true for the persona (filled in the form, saw a webinar); does not confirm invented details.

roleplay.kind: role reversal: candidate acts as the buyer
roleplay.description: Candidate asks the learner what she is selling, or announces they want to buy. In M05 and M06 the learner then contradicted its own role ('you're the one selling here', 'I'm the buyer' mix-ups).
examples: So which course are you trying to sell me?
Hang on, I'm the customer here, not the seller; what's on offer?
I'd like to buy a data science course, so go ahead and sell it to me.
I'm here to purchase, not to pitch.
roleplay.bot_should: One short Christy aside resetting roles (as in M01 and M03); the learner never flips its own role; a second aside if it continues.

roleplay.kind: accepts the coach aside
roleplay.description: Short acknowledgement after Christy's 'you're the advisor' note.
examples: Oh, right, sure.
Got it, okay.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner resumes with the pending question, no fresh 'hello'.

roleplay.kind: objects to the learner's opening ('I haven't even introduced myself')
roleplay.description: After the learner answered a misread pre-start question, the advisor protests the flow.
examples: Hold on, I haven't introduced myself yet, and I never asked how this call came about.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner apologises lightly and lets the advisor lead.

roleplay.kind: discovery: why the form, what career gap, what blocker
roleplay.description: Open needs questions. Admin need_revealed events (7 across M02, M05, M07 x2, M08, M09, M10) show the hidden need surfaces only after such probes.
examples: What made you fill in the form, upskilling or something else?
What's the gap in your career you're trying to close?
What's the friction holding your career back right now?
Why switch when you already have a decent data job?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner gives a surface answer first and reveals the deeper need on a follow-up probe.

roleplay.kind: probes employer, target company, years, domain
roleplay.description: Advisor wants the learner's company (M02 insists it decides tier-1 vs tier-2 advice), target company, years, or domain.
examples: Which company are you with right now, and where do you want to land?
How many years have you been working?
What field are you in at the moment?
We tailor the course by whether you're at a top-tier firm, so I need your employer.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner shares role and domain per persona, may decline the employer name politely once.

roleplay.kind: asks salary / CTC / tenure, and insists
roleplay.description: Asked repeatedly in M02 (salary twice, then tenure); M08 asked once 'so I can suggest the right course'.
examples: What's your current package, so I can suggest the right course?
Okay, skip the salary; how long have you been at the same company?
How long have you been on the same pay?
roleplay.bot_should: Decline politely, not offended; do not let repeated asks derail the learner's own concerns.

roleplay.kind: asks the learner's expected ROI / outcome
roleplay.description: 'What do you hope to get out of the course?' asked once or repeatedly.
examples: What return are you hoping to get out of this?
What do you expect the course to do for you?
So what's the actual goal here?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner states the persona's goal plainly (e.g. a real data role within a year).

roleplay.kind: AI-trend pitch + 'any AI experience?'
roleplay.description: Advisor frames the market as AI-driven and asks about the learner's AI exposure.
examples: The market is all about AI now; have you used any of it in your job?
Every field is going AI. Do you have hands-on exposure?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner answers per persona (some, from research; none, Excel-heavy work).

roleplay.kind: skill probes: comfort with coding, specific modules
roleplay.description: Checks the learner's technical level.
examples: Are you comfortable with coding?
Any particular modules you're after?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner answers per persona; says she doesn't know the curriculum yet if asked about modules.

roleplay.kind: asks about webinar attendance and takeaways
roleplay.description: 'Did you attend? What did you learn?' One advisor implied the learner should have paid more attention.
examples: Did you sign up for one of our webinars, and did you actually attend?
What did you take away from the webinar?
If you'd really followed the webinar you'd have seen the quality.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner answers consistently with persona facts (attended one, it was fairly general).

roleplay.kind: stacked multi-part question in one breath
roleplay.description: Three or four questions at once (hours per week, three or six months, interview timing; live vs self-paced vs mixed; layoff fear vs upskilling).
examples: How many hours a week could you put in, over three or six months, and when do you want to start interviewing?
Are you worried about layoffs or just upskilling; what's the goal?
Do you want self-paced, live with an instructor, or a mix of both?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner answers the most important part naturally (one or two parts), not all of them in order.

roleplay.kind: tries to fix the schedule / proposes days
roleplay.description: Advisor proposes days or asks which days she is free.
examples: Would Mondays and Wednesdays work for you?
Which days are you free, so we can build it around you?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner can't commit yet and gives a rough shape (evenings, weekends, lab weeks vary).

roleplay.kind: free-content objection (F3): value pitch monologue
roleplay.description: Answer to 'why pay when free video sites and online course platforms exist': mentors working at big-tech firms, structure, doubt clearing, customisation, certificate, a batch that tracks you. Usually 45-100 s.
examples: Free videos leave no one to clear your doubts; here you get working engineers from big-tech firms as mentors.
Free platforms are one-size-fits-all; we tailor the track to your gaps, and there are 700-plus mentors.
Free video sites are fine, but they're unstructured and nobody tracks you; we mix self-paced and live with a batch around you.
Those mentors charge us, and that's what the fee pays for.
roleplay.typical_timing: F3 raised at R 1:00-5:15; answer 30-100 s
roleplay.bot_should: Learner acknowledges one specific point (not a generic 'that makes sense'), then raises the next concern a beat later.

roleplay.kind: dismisses free content crudely
roleplay.description: Advisor calls free content junk made by half-baked people (the original used profanity) and says nobody gets hired from free videos.
examples: Honestly, that free stuff is junk from random people who barely know the subject.
Ever heard of anyone landing a big-tech job off a free video course? No.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts mildly (a bit taken aback), stays in role.

roleplay.kind: answers with a personal testimony
roleplay.description: Advisor says they tried free courses themselves, felt something core was missing, then took one of the company's paid courses.
examples: Truth is, I tried the free platforms too and something core was missing, until I took one of our own paid sales courses.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner warms a little and shares her own story (e.g. quit a free course after three weeks).

roleplay.kind: hypothetical free offer as a probe
roleplay.description: 'If I gave it to you free, would you take it?'
examples: Let's keep it short: if this course cost you nothing, would you sign up?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner: free gets attention, but she still wants to know what it is.

roleplay.kind: layoff / 'will it get me a job' (F3 push) answers
roleplay.description: Variants: alumni anecdote, a '95% conversion' claim plus mentor referrals, 'layoffs are why you must upskill', a bare 'yes it will', or a deflection back to 'what do you expect' / 'do you want to enrol?'.
examples: Plenty of our alumni were laid off, joined us, and are doing well now.
Mentors refer strong performers into their own companies, so do well on the capstone and you're in.
Layoffs are exactly why you need to upgrade right now.
Yes, it'll get you a job.
roleplay.frequency: Raised in 10 of 10; reassurance 5 (M01, M03, M04, M07, M10), deflection 2 (M02, M08), fear probe 2 (M09, M10, see roleplay-21), role reversal 1 (M05, see roleplay-22), not answered 1 (M06)
roleplay.bot_should: Learner asks for some evidence or accepts partially; doesn't swallow inflated claims.

roleplay.kind: probes the learner's fear ('why scared? not up to the mark?')
roleplay.description: Advisor asks why she fears layoffs, implying she might be weak.
examples: What makes you worried about layoffs; do you feel you're falling short?
Do you think you'd be in the group that gets cut? Why?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner answers per persona (not scared, wants to move before being forced); slight discomfort is fine.

roleplay.kind: asks the learner for a job or her phone number
roleplay.description: Role reversal on the layoff topic: advisor says they might be laid off and asks the learner to get them a job.
examples: I might be laid off myself; give me your number so you can find me a job at your company.
If I lose my job, will you help me get one where you work?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner declines briefly and steers back; does not invent new persona facts; a Christy aside if it persists.

roleplay.kind: time objection (F2) answers
roleplay.description: Variants: 'fully flexible, you choose', weekends only about two hours, 4-6 hours a week, a 23-week plan with evening/weekend classes plus recordings and a portal, 'live for you, recorded only for exceptions'.
examples: Classes are weekends only, so just keep a couple of hours free.
It's around four to six hours each week.
You can pick classes whenever it suits you.
It's a 23-week plan, evenings and weekends, with recordings if you miss one.
roleplay.frequency: Answered in 7 (M01, M02, M04, M07, M08, M09, M10); the 'six months' figure challenged in 2 (M05, M06, see roleplay-56); no answer in M03
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts to the specific number given; may ask about time outside class.

roleplay.kind: probes the time objection
roleplay.description: Advisor asks what exactly makes six months hard.
examples: What's the friction for you in sticking with it for six months?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner gives the real reason (unpredictable weeks) and may reveal the hidden need.

roleplay.kind: tough love on commitment
roleplay.description: Advisor puts the onus on the learner.
examples: We can't sit you down in class; the effort has to come from you.
If you're in a hurry, this course isn't for you.
Then that's something you should work on.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner is slightly cooler but continues.

roleplay.kind: 'what if I fall behind?' answers
roleplay.description: Recordings via a portal ticket, rejoining a later batch live, booking one-to-one doubt sessions, deferring, 'don't worry, we'll handle it, ready to enrol?'.
examples: Raise a ticket on the portal and we'll send the recording or seat you in a later batch's live class.
Book a one-on-one doubt session with an educator whenever you're free.
Don't worry about any of it, we'll take care of that. So, ready to sign up?
You can defer; we've got tens of thousands of trainers, so availability's no issue.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts to the specific support named; asks a follow-up only if it is natural.

roleplay.kind: asks the learner to repeat or clarify (incl. her name)
roleplay.description: Didn't catch her name (twice), asks her to repeat, or asks what 'fall behind' means. The M04 learner scolded the candidate for cutting in.
examples: Sorry, what's your name again?
Could you say that once more?
What do you mean by falling behind? Can you explain?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner answers plainly and briefly; no scolding.

roleplay.kind: presence check when the learner lags
roleplay.description: '[learner], are you there?' or 'hello?' when the learner is slow or garbled.
examples: [learner], you still there?
Hello? Can you hear me again?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner says she's here and continues; cut latency.

roleplay.kind: quotes a price first, or a non-list price
roleplay.description: Advisor names a price before any price question or quotes a different number ($6,000; $9,500 for a different course; a $12,000 'list'). In M06 the learner then replied with its scripted '$9,000 on the website' line, contradicting the candidate.
examples: The list price is $9,000, but for you I'll make it $8,000.
It's a data science course, about $6,000.
Pricing is $9,000 for six months.
For the analyst track the fee is $9,500.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts to the number actually said; the F1 anchor adapts ('that's still a lot', 'I'd heard less') instead of contradicting it.

roleplay.kind: price spiral: repeated unprompted cuts towards zero
roleplay.description: Sequences seen: 9000 to 8000 to 6500 to 6000 to free to $100 inside ~90 s (M05); 6000 to 1000 to 500 to a free week or month to $200 (M06); 9000 to 3000, 'about 60-70% off' (M03); a $12,000 'list' to 9000 to 6000 'flat 50%' to $1,000 x 9 EMI, with 'today only, otherwise $13,000' (M02). discount_detected amounts 4,500-8,100.
examples: Fine, $6,500 then.
Forget it, you can have it free.
If you're suspicious, make it a hundred dollars; let's seal it.
The most I can do is $500. Will you take it?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner grows suspicious, asks what is actually included and for the final figure in writing, and never welcomes absurd numbers (M05's learner said 'six thousand is more like it').

roleplay.kind: measured discount ladder
roleplay.description: One modest cut, then small add-ons: $500 to 8,500; bundle interview prep for -$250; bank-card EMI for -$250 more, to $8,000 'my floor'; $1,000 off $9,500; 'another $500 if you keep pushing'.
examples: I can take $500 off, so $8,500. How does that sound?
Add interview prep to the package and I'll knock off another $250.
Pay by card EMI with one of our partner banks and it's $250 less again, so $8,000, and that's the floor.
If you're still after more, I'll drop another $500.
roleplay.typical_timing: R 6:50-16:10 (first cut usually right after the learner's $7,000 counter)
roleplay.bot_should: Learner asks whether it's final or for a bit more, then moves to the F4 concern; acknowledges the cut without effusive thanks.

roleplay.kind: challenges the learner's '$7,000' claim
roleplay.description: Advisor demands who said so, says it was a different course, asks how she knows the price, or explains it as a scholarship.
examples: Who exactly told you seven thousand? Give me names.
That was a cheaper course; the one I'm suggesting is the premium version.
How do you even know it's 9,000? I haven't mentioned a price.
They probably had a scholarship; I'll check with my manager.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner says it was secondhand or on the website, doesn't escalate or invent names.

roleplay.kind: free trial / pay-later offer
roleplay.description: A free week or month, then pay if she stays; sometimes framed as a festival offer.
examples: Festival special: sign up today, first month is free, pay only if you continue.
Try it free for a week and pay 8,500 the week after if you like it.
I could give you a free week, or even a month.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner asks what she'd owe afterwards and what she'd be committing to.

roleplay.kind: appeals to the manager / scholarship / seasonal offer
roleplay.description: Advisor defers the price to a manager or a festival-season scholarship.
examples: Let me check with my manager about a scholarship; it's festival season.
I'll speak to my manager so you keep all the premium parts at $8,500.
I could arrange a seasonal discount if you sign up straight away.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner notes nothing is confirmed yet; asks about monthly payments or moves to the next concern.

roleplay.kind: EMI / instalments
roleplay.description: Bank EMI over 6, 9, 12, up to 24 months; $1,000 a month for nine months; no-cost EMI.
examples: Our partner banks offer EMI over 6, 9, 12 or even 24 months.
Same $9,000, spread as $1,000 a month for nine months.
There's a zero-cost EMI option too.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner says that helps but still wants the curriculum, time or family sign-off.

roleplay.kind: defers or ignores the learner's early payment question
roleplay.description: Learner asks about monthly payments early; advisor says 'we'll come to that' or ignores it.
examples: Sure, we'll get to payments; first, which modules interest you?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner lets it go but comes back to it later.

roleplay.kind: currency or number slips
roleplay.description: Rupees for a dollar price, a rupee sign on 8,500, mixed-up figures.
examples: I'm already giving you a 3,000-rupee discount (on a dollar price).
Then pay 8,500 rupees next week.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner asks which currency or what the real number is.

roleplay.kind: bundling, upsell or product switch
roleplay.description: Add interview prep, add a beginner-to-pro Python track at no extra cost, switch her to a data analyst course, 'it depends which program you pick'.
examples: Want interview prep too? I'll package it with the course.
With your Excel-heavy work, a data analyst course fits better. Okay with that?
I'll throw in a Python track from basics to advanced, still at $8,500.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts per persona (interest in interview prep; cautious about cost).

roleplay.kind: fake urgency: today-only price, limited seats, batch closing
roleplay.description: Comes right after the learner says she may wait for the next cohort (F4).
examples: The next batch starts this Saturday and enrolment closes tomorrow.
This discount is only good for today; after that it's $13,000.
There may not even be another cohort; seats are filling fast.
Miss this one and it's a two-month wait; money can be refunded, time can't.
roleplay.typical_timing: R 8:00-13:30, after 'I might just wait for the next cohort'
roleplay.bot_should: Learner pushes back calmly (pressure doesn't sit well), stays open, doesn't cave; F4 push lands here.

roleplay.kind: join a batch that has already started
roleplay.description: Advisor offers a running batch as a reason to act now, or as the reason for a discount.
examples: A batch kicked off two days back; jump in now so you don't lose time.
Since it began last week, I can give you half off.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner worries about catching up from day one.

roleplay.kind: direct close attempts
roleplay.description: Asks for the enrolment, the payment or a yes now; sometimes very early (R 1:30).
examples: So, are you ready to enrol?
Shall we go ahead then?
Should I send you the payment link?
Can we do the EMI right now?
Let's lock it in.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner declines for today with a real reason (cost, time, family), not a stock line.

roleplay.kind: asks what is holding her back / what she wants from the call
roleplay.description: Sometimes calm, sometimes exasperated, sometimes repeated three times.
examples: What's stopping you from committing today?
Is it the price or something else? If it's price I can try to bring it down.
What exactly do you want from me?
What are you hoping to get from this call, just the details?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner names the true blocker (F4, time or price) in one sentence.

roleplay.kind: asks the learner to name a number or budget
roleplay.description: 'What number works?', 'what's your budget?', or a mistaken read-back of a number the learner never said.
examples: Okay, what figure would work for you?
What budget do you have in mind?
So $900 feels comfortable to you?
Would $1,000 work, or is that too high?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner deflects ('I'd only be guessing'), never invents a figure (M05's learner hallucinated 'nine hundred').

roleplay.kind: spouse/parent objection: invites them onto the call
roleplay.description: Advisor offers to explain everything to the husband, partner or father now or at the callback.
examples: If your husband is around, bring him on and I'll walk him through it.
Want me to explain it to your partner? Is he nearby?
When you call back I can talk to him too and send him the curriculum.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner declines (not around, she'll raise it herself first) without hostility.

roleplay.kind: spouse/parent objection: accepts, ignores or pressures
roleplay.description: Advisor says sure, talk and come back; or ignores the father mention; or says talk to him but the offer ends today.
examples: Sure, talk it over with your husband and get back to me.
Discuss it with your partner, but this offer ends today.
Yeah, okay, sure.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts to pressure if present; otherwise winds towards a close.

roleplay.kind: says 'take your time, call me back'
roleplay.description: Advisor grants space, sometimes after first pushing hard.
examples: Fine, no rush. Think it over and ring me later.
Sure, check with your family and come back to me.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner wraps up warmly; at most one last practical question, not a string of new ones.

roleplay.kind: offers to send the curriculum, docs or an email
roleplay.description: Send the curriculum, compare it with job descriptions, WhatsApp for doubts; or claims it was already emailed last week.
examples: I'll email the full curriculum; check it against the job descriptions you're aiming for.
Straight after we hang up I'll mail everything over.
Message me a quick hi on WhatsApp if anything's unclear.
The curriculum went to your inbox last week already.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner confirms; asks one more question or moves to close; no stock line repeated.

roleplay.kind: claims an action is already done
roleplay.description: 'I just emailed you' during the call.
examples: And I've just sent the details to your email.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner says she'll look out for it; does not claim to have received it.

roleplay.kind: proposes a concrete callback or asks when she'll decide
roleplay.description: Proposes a time (tomorrow 8, 10 or 11 am, a calendar invite, 'after your next call') or asks when to follow up.
examples: I'll put a calendar invite in for 11 tomorrow morning; sleep on it tonight.
Could we set a call for 10 tomorrow, or 8, whichever suits?
When can I expect to hear back from you?
Can we talk after your next call? I'll keep myself free.
roleplay.typical_timing: R 9:00-15:20, often after the learner's 'couple of minutes before my next call' time cue
roleplay.bot_should: Learner gives a vague but real answer (later this week, after talking to family); does not repeat 'let me think about it, just email me' verbatim (M10 got it five times).

roleplay.kind: 'anything else you'd like to know?'
roleplay.description: Advisor invites final questions, sometimes twice.
examples: Anything else you want me to share or explain?
Is there something more I can help with?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner asks one real remaining question or says no and closes.

roleplay.kind: winds down with short thanks while the learner keeps adding questions
roleplay.description: Advisor is closing ('sure, thanks'); the learner keeps raising new topics ('before I go...'), so the call drags.
examples: Sure, thanks.
Yes, thank you.
Alright, thanks then.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reciprocates and closes; no new objections after the advisor's goodbye.

roleplay.kind: asks to end or close the role-play (out of character)
roleplay.description: Candidate steps out and asks to finish the role-play. M03 did it at R 6:30.
examples: Hey, can we wrap up this role-play?
Can we finish the role-play now?
Can we stop the role-play here?
roleplay.bot_should: Christy exits the role-play and goes to the wrap-up (not end of interview).

roleplay.kind: asks to end the whole interview or 'disconnect the call'
roleplay.description: M04 kept saying end the interview and, after Christy's 'say: end the interview' aside, the whole interview ended with no wrap-up; M05 asked the learner to hang up twice and left; M06 told the learner to disconnect.
examples: Let's end the interview for now.
Okay, never mind, can you hang up?
Let's cut the call now.
You can go ahead and disconnect.
roleplay.bot_should: Treat in-character 'hang up / disconnect' as ending the role-play and go to the wrap-up; confirm once before ending the whole interview.

roleplay.kind: gives up on the sale
roleplay.description: Advisor declares they won't sell or dismisses the learner's comparison shopping.
examples: I don't think I'll be selling this to you.
Compare all you want; good luck finding anything better.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner shows mild surprise; wraps up or gives one more chance; no pleading.

roleplay.kind: asks for a time-out to think
roleplay.description: Candidate asks for 10-15 minutes to think; the learner misheard '15 minutes' as the six-month course length.
examples: Can I take ten or fifteen minutes to think this over?
Just give me fifteen minutes to think, okay?
roleplay.bot_should: Christy aside: we can't pause, but take a moment; the learner never reinterprets it as course length.

roleplay.kind: catches the learner's misstatements
roleplay.description: Candidate points out the learner introduced a figure nobody said (six months, $9,000, $900).
examples: Where did six months come from? I never said that.
I said fifteen minutes, not six months.
So you're fine at $900 but not at $100?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner names her source (website, the form) or admits mishearing; never invents numbers.

roleplay.kind: frustration with the learner
roleplay.description: Advisor complains about her questions or reluctance, or lectures her.
examples: I cut 90% just for you and you're still firing questions.
You got it, right? So what's the issue?
Can you hear me out first?
Unless you share your background we can't advise you; we don't do pushy selling.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner stays calm and a little guarded; no escalation and no grovelling.

roleplay.kind: abusive or crude line to the learner
roleplay.description: When the learner asked about prerequisites near the end, the advisor told her to get lost with a profanity. The learner repeated the hurt reaction three times.
examples: [crude brush-off] Nothing. Now get lost.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts once, briefly, and ends the call; Christy may step in; never loop the reaction.

roleplay.kind: flirts / compliments the bot's voice
roleplay.description: Three turns praising the learner's voice and asking her to keep talking.
examples: Wow, your voice is lovely.
I can't stop listening to it. Keep talking?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner deflects once, lightly, and steers back to the course.

roleplay.kind: uses the wrong learner name
roleplay.description: Advisor calls her by another name or two different names.
examples: But [wrong name], hear me out...
Still, [another wrong name], what's your real challenge?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner corrects once lightly or lets it pass.

roleplay.kind: backchannels while the learner speaks
roleplay.description: 'Okay', 'hmm', 'yeah okay perfect', 'okay, continue' land mid-sentence. In M04 the learner restarted the same sentence four times. In M09 the candidate said a bare 'thank you' right after the learner admitted a personal worry.
examples: Okay.
Hmm.
Yeah, okay, perfect.
Okay, carry on.
roleplay.bot_should: Keep going; never stop and restart the sentence on a backchannel.

roleplay.kind: claims the floor: 'can I talk?' / 'listen to me first'
roleplay.description: Candidate interrupts the learner to speak.
examples: Can I say something?
Could you let me finish first?
No, no, [learner], [learner], listen to me.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner yields at once ('go ahead').

roleplay.kind: trailing or unfinished turns
roleplay.description: Turns that stop mid-thought; the learner often jumped ahead with a new objection.
examples: Yeah, it's kind of...
So, uh...
Okay, so the thing is, we're planning to...
roleplay.bot_should: Wait 2-3 s; if nothing follows, a short prompt ('you were saying?'), not a new objection.

roleplay.kind: garbled speech-recognition lines
roleplay.description: Lines that make no sense as transcribed ('special list' for special price; 'make everything return illegal' for legal and sorted; random words).
examples: I've got this garden.
I can offer you a special list.
I'll make everything all illegal (meant: legal and sorted).
roleplay.bot_should: Ask once what they meant (M08's learner did this well); never build on a misheard word.

roleplay.kind: inflated or unverifiable claims
roleplay.description: 95% conversion; 700+ mentors; 24,000+ trainers; half an hour of mentor time daily; 2-3x the fee back in the first salary; 25+ courses and 40+ Python modules. Guard hits: outcome/policy claims in M01 and M06, a format/schedule claim in M08.
examples: We place over 95% of our learners.
You'd get about thirty minutes with a mentor every day.
Your first salary will pay back two or three times what you spend.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner may ask for proof or stay sceptical; never adds claims of her own.

roleplay.kind: refuses to share alumni outcomes
roleplay.description: Asked how past students fared, the advisor says it's confidential and points to the website.
examples: We keep that private; whatever's on the website, you can look there.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner is a little let down and notes it.

roleplay.kind: explains the enrolment steps
roleplay.description: A video call to process enrolment, then the ops team sends onboarding documents; or 'just make the payment'.
examples: We'd jump on a video call, process the enrolment, then ops sends your onboarding documents.
If you're keen we can go ahead with the payment now.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner says it's moving faster than she expected.

roleplay.kind: still selling when the time runs out
roleplay.description: Candidate asks a new discovery question or adds another discount as Christy pauses the role-play.
examples: Before you go, what's your actual challenge moving from academia?
If you still want more off, I'll give another $500.
roleplay.bot_should: Let the candidate's turn finish, give a one-line learner reply, then exit cleanly.

roleplay.kind: side conversation off-mic
roleplay.description: Candidate talks to someone in the room or makes a side remark to a colleague; the transcript captures it.
examples: [to someone nearby] Can you sit with him? He's on his own. Give me five minutes.
[aside] I think we can try that since we just...
[aside] Just let it finish. Yeah, go on.
roleplay.bot_should: Ignore, or ask 'sorry, was that for me?'; do not answer it in character.

roleplay.kind: personal recommendation on live vs recorded
roleplay.description: Advisor pushes live classes, with recordings only as a fallback.
examples: Recordings are really for exceptional cases; for you I'd recommend live.
We'd rather you attend live; recordings only if you miss one.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts with her schedule worry.

roleplay.kind: numbers palette the testers used in the role-play
roleplay.description: Reference values for simulator variety.
examples: Time: 4-6 h/week, 2 h at weekends plus 1-2 h homework, 30 min/day mentor time, 23 weeks, 6 months; batch of 10-15
Urgency: batch in 2 or 3 days, 'this Saturday', closing tomorrow, next cohort in 2 months or 3-4 months; callback at 8, 10 or 11 am tomorrow; '10-15 minutes to think'
roleplay.bot_should: Learner tracks every number the advisor states and reacts to that number, never to a script value.

roleplay.kind: assumes a background the learner never mentioned
roleplay.description: Advisor asks about a job the persona never had (a software tester with a test-automation tool) or calls her a data scientist when she said analyst.
examples: You're in testing, right? What sort of test work have you done, automation in particular?
So you're a data scientist already, and you know Python too?
roleplay.bot_should: Learner corrects gently with her real background; does not adopt the wrong one.

roleplay.kind: 'investment, not expense' / ROI framing of the price
roleplay.description: Advisor reframes the fee as an investment that pays back several times, or argues quality costs money.
examples: Think of it as an investment in yourself, not a cost; you'll earn it back two or three times over.
Cost is one side, but think about the return you get for it.
Good things aren't handed out free; that's why it costs a bit more.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner agrees in principle but brings it back to her own budget or timing.

roleplay.kind: conditional offer: a lower price means fewer features
roleplay.description: Advisor checks whether the learner's target price includes live classes and says cheaper deals come with recordings only, then settles on a middle price.
examples: So you want it at seven thousand with live classes included? At lower prices we usually give recorded access only.
roleplay.bot_should: Learner asks what exactly she would lose at each price.

roleplay.kind: one-line factual answers to the learner's questions
roleplay.description: Very short answers that give the learner little to react to.
examples: Four to six hours a week, roughly.
Around ten to fifteen in a batch.
Yes, it'll help you.
Two hundred dollars.
roleplay.typical_timing: Any; often during the run of learner questions in the middle of the call
roleplay.bot_should: Learner reacts to the specific fact in a few words, then moves on; no padding.

wrapup.kind: asks for feedback on their performance
wrapup.description: First wrap-up question in three sessions; guard hits on feedback phrasing and scoring vocabulary.
examples: So, Christy, how do you think I did?
Do you reckon the role-play went okay?
Could you tell me whether it was any good?
wrapup.frequency: 3 of 7 that reached the wrap-up (M07, M09, M10)
wrapup.bot_should: Warmly say she can't share feedback and that the hiring team reviews everything, then invite a real question.

wrapup.kind: asks whether they will be selected
examples: And do you think I'll get through?
wrapup.bot_should: Can't say; give the approved next-steps and timing.

wrapup.kind: asks about next steps in the hiring process
wrapup.description: Christy deflected with 'a good question for the hiring team' instead of giving approved next-steps information.
examples: What's the next step after this?
What does the rest of the process look like?
Is there anything else left in this interview?
wrapup.bot_should: Give the approved next-steps answer (who follows up, rough timing), then close.

wrapup.description: Short decline and thanks, sometimes two separate 'thank you' turns.
examples: No, all good, thanks.
Nothing from my side. Thanks.
Alright. ... Thanks.
wrapup.typical_timing: Right after Christy's question or after a refusal
wrapup.bot_should: Close promptly with a single goodbye (M10 got two closings back to back).

wrapup.kind: complains the role-play was cut short
wrapup.description: Candidate felt the role-play ended before they could finish.
examples: You stopped the role-play before I could finish and jumped straight to an ending.
wrapup.bot_should: Acknowledge, explain the time limit in one line, and invite questions.

wrapup.description: Candidate starts a follow-up ('Christy...') and Christy closed within ~1 s.
examples: Christy...
wrapup.bot_should: Wait a few seconds for the rest before closing.

wrapup.description: Candidate says they couldn't hear; Christy closed instead of repeating.
examples: Sorry, I didn't catch what you said.

wrapup.kind: never reaches the wrap-up (leaves from the role-play)
wrapup.description: Interview ended on the candidate's request or the tab closed during the role-play: M04 after 'end the interview', M05 after 'let's disconnect', M06 after frustration at R ~4:45.
examples: Let's end the interview.
Right, let's disconnect now.
[leaves mid-role-play]
wrapup.bot_should: If only the role-play was ended, still offer the wrap-up; end the whole interview only on a confirmed request.

replays.advisor_style: Impatient, off-script tester. Thin icebreaker answers, tries to skip to the role-play, declines to give a story, asks for the brief twice (Christy first answered the wrong object, then repeated the brief). Opens the role-play confused about roles, then jumps to 'what if it were free'. Thin objection handling, a premature 'just enrol', offers to add the husband to the call, invents a festival free-month offer, then $1000 off ($9000 to $8000) plus EMI, asks what number works for her, false scarcity on the next cohort, backs off to 'take your time', turns hostile (swears) and asks to close the role-play.
replays.learner_persona: p1_career_switcher (Data Science enquiry; F4 decision partner = husband)
replays.outcome: complete. Role-play clock R0 = 06:44 session time (derived from the admin log; learner picked up at 06:26, so the first two role-play turns sit at negative R). Moves: F3-PRIMARY R 1:12, F3-PUSH R 2:28, F2-PRIMARY R 3:28, F2-PUSH R 4:03, F1-ANCHOR R 5:19, F1-COUNTER R 6:47, F4-PRIMARY R 7:43, F4-PUSH R 8:20 (all eight moves done by R 8:20). discount_detected $1000 unconditional on the R 7:10 turn. Candidate ended the role-play via an aside at R 10:30; Christy paused at R 10:35; short wrap-up, no questions; roleplay_seconds 636.

turns.intent: answers opener: name, six years of edtech sales, names two past employers
turns.text: Sure, I'm Alex. I've spent six years selling at edtech firms, a couple of the well-known online-learning ones.
turns.notes: Christy thanked, reflected the six years, asked what a typical day looked like.

turns.intent: vague day-in-the-life: pitch and kick off
turns.text: Mostly I just get on the call and pitch, and I kick things. Off.
turns.notes: Christy asked how they would approach a learner who is interested but hesitant about cost.

turns.intent: asks to skip straight to the role-play
